Who should get the women's email?

Detailed, plain-language guide to the team project (v2). For the whole team. Every v2 number is read from outputs_v2/results.json, v1 numbers from the untouched outputs/results.json. Rebuild with uv run python make_guide.py.

Overview

1. The short version

A retailer can email only 15.6% of its customers. We tested seven ways to pick them, using a real experiment where emails were sent at random.

Uplift models vs RFM, visits
+2.2 pp
X-learner minus RFM [0.3, 4.2]. Clear win.
Uplift model vs one-line rule
+0.4 pp
X-learner minus women's rule [-1.6, 2.3]. No clear difference.
Best on spend
RFM $1.07
per listed customer [$0.31, $1.92]. Wide interval.
Break-even cost per email
$0.54
RFM, assumed 50% margin. v1 assumed $5.

Five things to remember

  1. Uplift beats RFM on visits. Ranking by past spend gives about the same extra visits as picking at random.
  2. A one-line rule matches the models. "Past women's buyers first, then by past spend" is as good as the T-learner and X-learner. The models largely rediscover this rule.
  3. RFM leads on spend, but it is uncertain. Spend is very noisy because 99.3% of customers spend nothing.
  4. v1's "X-learner wins" came from one lucky split. On 20 other splits the same pipeline did worse.
  5. With two emails, the email choice matters as much as targeting. The men's email to random customers did about as well as the targeted women's list.

How to read this page

Badges show where each piece comes from:

  • NEW Added in v2, during this upgrade.
  • FROM V1 Already in the repo before v2. This page only describes it.
  • CHANGED Existed in v1 and was modified in v2.

Tags show what kind of statement it is: FACT a design fact about the data, RESULT produced by our code, ASSUMPTION a choice we made that is not in the data, SPECULATION our interpretation.

A difference marked clear has a 95% interval that does not include zero. not clear means the data cannot tell the two apart.

The problem and the data

3. The problem CHANGED

FACT The course brief: an organisation has more opportunities than it can pursue. Which ones should it choose, and how do you show the choice is good?

Our setting: an apparel retailer sends a women's-merchandise email. Its contact policy allows emailing at most q = 15.6% of customers in one campaign. That is 10,000 of 64,000, the number in the dataset author's own challenge question ("the best 10,000 customers"). ASSUMPTION

Brief termOur project
OrganisationAn online apparel retailer
OpportunitiesCustomers who could receive the email
Limit Kq = 15.6% of customers. In our evaluation sample that is 6,670 of 42,693.
Good decisionMaximise extra website visits caused by the email (primary). Extra spend is secondary.
RankingEach policy scores customers. The top q get the email.

Response vs uplift, with an example

Imagine two customers:

CustomerVisits if emailedVisits if not emailedEffect of the email
A loyal regular90%85%+5 pp
B occasional buyer40%20%+20 pp

A response model ranks A first because A is more likely to visit. An uplift model ranks B first because the email changes B's behaviour more. With a limited number of emails, B is the better use of one. (Illustrative numbers, not from the data.)

What changed in the framing CHANGED

v1 framed the decision as "contact 1,500 of 12,808 at an assumed $5 per contact". Two problems:

  • No list earned anywhere near $5 per contact, so at that cost the best list size is zero.
  • The experiment tested an email, not a $5 catalog. The $5 was not measured anywhere.

v2 uses a contact cap instead and reports break-even cost per email under an explicit margin assumption. The old setting is still reported for continuity.

Why a random experiment lets us score any list

We never see one person both emailed and not emailed. But the email was random. So inside any list chosen using only pre-email fields, about half the people were emailed and half were not, by chance. The two halves are alike in every other way. So: visit rate of the emailed half minus visit rate of the not-emailed half = the effect of the email on that list. This is how we score a list without inventing any ground truth.

Balance check FROM V1

RESULT If randomisation worked, the arms should look alike before the email. Standardised mean difference (SMD) below 0.10 is the usual threshold. All 8 of 8 fields pass. Largest: 0.014.

The model settings FROM V1

All models use scikit-learn's HistGradientBoosting (HGB), a tree-boosting model, with the v1 settings:

ModelIterationsMax leavesLearning rateL2 penalty
Classifier (visit models)120150.071.0
Regressor (X-learner effect models)100100.052.0

Nothing was tuned. Tuning on the same data we evaluate on would make the models look better than they are.

How the X-learner works, step by step FROM V1
  1. Fit a visit model on emailed customers, m1(x), and one on not-emailed customers, m0(x). Both are isotonic-calibrated with 5 internal folds.
  2. For each emailed customer, estimate their personal effect as: actual visit minus m0(x). This fills in "what if not emailed" with the other arm's model.
  3. For each not-emailed customer: m1(x) minus actual visit.
  4. Fit a regressor to each set of personal effects: tau1(x) and tau0(x).
  5. Blend: score = e x tau0(x) + (1 minus e) x tau1(x), where e is the share emailed (about one half).

The T-learner skips steps 2 to 5 and uses m1(x) minus m0(x) directly.

Why add the women's-buyer rules? NEW

The email is a women's-merchandise email. Past women's buyers are the obvious target. In v1, the X-learner's list was almost entirely women's buyers. If a one-line rule does as well as the model, the model adds little. The brief asks exactly this ("could a simple rule achieve much of your result?").

RESULT In v2's lists, 99.5% of the X-learner list and 96.7% of the T-learner list are past women's buyers.

Method and results

6. How we tested them NEW

The evaluation, step by step NEW

  1. Split the 42,693 customers into 5 equal folds. The split keeps the mix of emailed/not and visited/not the same in every fold (stratified).
  2. For each fold: train every model on the other 4 folds, then score this fold. Every customer gets a score from models that never saw them.
  3. Inside each fold, rank customers and take the top 15.6%. Combine the five lists: 6,670 customers.
  4. Inside the combined list: visit rate of emailed minus visit rate of not emailed = visit lift. Same for spend.
  5. Repeat steps 1 to 4 with 5 different random fold splits (fold seeds 0 to 4). Report the mean and SD.
  6. For the canonical split (seed 0): draw 2,000 bootstrap samples. Each resamples customers with replacement inside each arm, keeping the lists fixed. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles give the 95% interval.
  7. Paired differences: on each bootstrap sample, compute policy A's lift minus policy B's lift. The interval of those differences says whether A really beats B.

Worked example: X-learner at the cap RESULT

EmailedNot emailedDifference
Customers in the list3,3033,367
Visit rate18.5%11.0%+7.5 pp
Spend per customer$1.23$0.61+$0.61

Same calculation for RFM: 18.9% vs 13.5%, lift +5.3 pp. For the women's rule: 21.8% vs 14.7%, lift +7.1 pp.

Formulas

QuantityFormula
Lift in a list Smean(outcome | S, emailed) minus mean(outcome | S, not emailed)
95% interval2.5th to 97.5th percentile of the lift over bootstrap samples
Paired difference A vs BOn each bootstrap sample: lift(A) minus lift(B). Interval from those values.
Break-even cost per emailmargin x spend lift
Sample size multiplier(2 x SE of paired difference / observed difference) squared
Jaccard overlap of lists A and Bcustomers in both / customers in either
SMD(mean emailed minus mean not emailed) / pooled SD

Design decisions and why NEW

DecisionWhy
Cap q = 10,000 / 64,000The dataset author's own question. A real, external number, not tuned.
Visits primary, spend secondaryVisits are common enough to measure differences. Spend is almost always zero, so it is too noisy to rank policies.
Cross-fitting, not one splitUses all customers for evaluation. One split left only about 750 per arm per list and was very luck-dependent.
Select top q inside each foldScores from different fold models may sit on different scales. Ranking within fold avoids mixing them.
Stratify folds on (treatment, visit)Keeps folds comparable. Visit is never a feature and never used to rank.
5 fold seedsShows how much results move when models are retrained on different data.
Bootstrap inside each arm, lists fixedMirrors the experiment's design. Same draws for all policies make comparisons paired and sharper.
Seeded tie-breaksMany customers share the same score (for example the rules). A random but seeded tie-break is fair and reproducible.
No tuningAvoids fitting the method to the evaluation data.
Keep the v1 X-learner exactlySo v2 can reproduce v1 and differences come only from the evaluation.
Margin 50%, with 30% and 60%Margin is not in the data. A round central value plus a sensitivity range.

What the intervals cover, and what they do not

  • The bootstrap interval covers outcome noise for the fixed lists: which customers happened to be in which arm.
  • It does not cover model noise: lists change when models are retrained on different folds. The SD across the 5 fold seeds shows that part.
  • Both are reported side by side in the results table.

Why the lists differ SPECULATION

  • RFM picks the biggest past spenders ($713 on average), many of whom buy both categories and use several channels. They spend more when emailed, but they would often visit anyway.

  • The X-learner picks lower past spenders ($318) who are almost all women's buyers.

9. Two-email extension NEW

Question: if the retailer could send either email to the same 15.6% of customers, which email, and to whom? Uses all 64,000 customers and all three arms.

How it works

  1. Cross-fit one visit model per arm (no email, women's, men's). Fold seed 0.
  2. Each policy decides, per customer: men's email, women's email or nothing. It contacts the top 15.6% in each fold.
  3. Score each policy by inverse-probability weighting (IPW): keep customers whose real random arm matches what the policy would send them. Weight each by 1 / (share of that arm). Normalise.
  4. Subtract the no-email result and divide by the share contacted. Result: extra visits and spend per contacted customer.
  5. Bootstrap 2,000 times, stratified by arm, for intervals and paired differences.

What it means. The men's email to a random list (+8.3 pp) is close to the targeted women's list (+7.9 pp). The difference is +0.3 pp [-2.1, 2.6]. So which email you send matters about as much as who gets it. The uplift models prefer the men's email for 74% of customers. Among the good policies, no gap is clear. Caution: one fold seed only, and this is an extension, not the main decision.

RESULT The raw data agrees: in the men's arm the visit rate is higher than in the women's arm. You can check this with the command in section 18.

Calibration CHANGED

Calibration adjusts predicted probabilities to match observed rates. It is a monotone map, so it cannot change the order of one model's scores. It does not change which customers a single model picks.

SettingSingle model BrierIsotonic Brier
v1 split (seed 42)0.125190.12547
v2 cross-fitted0.125550.12543

Lower is better. Differences are tiny and change sign. Also, the isotonic version averages five models, so it mixes calibration with averaging.

How much do features explain? NEW

RESULT Out of fold, the arm visit models explain 2.7% of the variation in visits (emailed arm 2.3%, not-emailed arm 2.3%). Visits are mostly unpredictable from these eight fields. That limits what any model can do, and is why regression adjustment (Arbour et al. 2026) would add little.

Back to top

13. What we cannot claim NEW

  • RESULT Model vs rule is unresolved. To separate them we would need about 22 times more customers for the X-learner, 5 times for the T-learner.
  • FACT No test over time. One campaign from 2008, a two-week window. We cannot check if rankings hold for the next campaign.
  • ASSUMPTION Spend is not profit. Margin, returns and email cost are not in the data.
  • FACT Email, not catalog. Costlier channels or offers may behave differently.
  • RESULT Little signal. Features explain 2.7% of visit variation.
  • FACT Two weeks only. No long-term value, repeat purchases or unsubscribes.
  • RESULT Intervals do not include model noise. Shown separately as SD across fold seeds.
  • RESULT Two-email results use one fold seed.
  • SPECULATION Next step. A larger random pilot of the women's rule vs the best model, with a no-email holdout and a margin field.

Q&A bank (22 questions) NEW

Click a question to see the answer. Same text as PRESENTER_NOTES.md.

Why is the cap 15.6%?

It is 10,000 of 64,000, the number in Hillstrom's own challenge question. It is configurable with --q. Results at other caps are in the robustness exhibit.

Why did you drop the $5 contact cost?

No list earned $5 per email in gross spend. At 50% margin the best break-even cost is $0.54 (RFM). At $5 the optimal list is empty. The data also tested an email, not a catalog.

Is a visit what the retailer values?

Not fully. A visit is a leading indicator of purchase. Visits are about 18 times as common as purchases, so they can be measured. Spend is closer to value but too noisy here to rank policies reliably.

Could a simple rule get most of the result?

Yes. The women's rule by history gets +7.1 pp. The X-learner gets +7.5 pp. The paired difference is +0.4 pp [-1.6, 2.3].

Then what does the model add?

On this data, nothing we can detect over the rule. It does beat RFM by +2.2 pp [0.3, 4.2]. The model also found the rule on its own: 99.5% of its list are women's buyers.

Why did v1 say the X-learner wins?

v1 used one split (seed 42). On 20 other splits the X-learner averaged 6.7 pp. Seed 42 ranked 1 of 21.

How do you know you did not overfit to the test data?

Model settings were copied from v1 and never tuned. The protocol was fixed in code before results were seen. Each customer is scored by a model that never saw them. All variants run are logged in outputs_v2/variants_tried.md.

What do your intervals cover?

Outcome noise given the lists, from 2,000 bootstrap draws resampling customers within each arm. Model retraining noise is shown separately as the SD over 5 fold seeds.

Why stratify the folds on visit? Is that leakage?

No. Stratification only balances fold sizes. Visit is never a feature and is never used to rank the held-out fold.

What was known at decision time?

Only the eight pre-campaign fields: recency, past spend, spend tier, men's and women's buyer flags, newbie, zip type and channel. Outcomes come from the two weeks after the email.

How many customers would you need to tell the model and the rule apart?

About 22 times as many for the X-learner, roughly 954,348, if the observed gap were real. About 5 times for the T-learner.

Why does RFM do well on spend but not on visits?

RFM picks big past spenders ($713 average). They spend more when emailed but often visit anyway. Its visit lift +5.3 pp is close to random +5.4 pp.

Is the spend difference between RFM and the X-learner real?

Not clearly. X-learner minus RFM on spend is -$0.46 [-$1.36, $0.41].

What is the break-even cost per email?

Margin x spend lift. At an assumed 50% margin: RFM $0.54 [$0.16, $0.96], rule $0.31, X-learner $0.31. Margin is an assumption. Spend is gross revenue.

Can you validate out of time?

No. There is one campaign from 2008 with a two-week window. This is the biggest gap for a real deployment.

Why not use a fancier model or tune it?

Features explain only about 2.7% of visit variance. The ceiling is low and tuning would add selection risk. A simple method carefully evaluated is the point.

What about calibration?

Calibration is a monotone map. It cannot change one model's ranking. Brier differences were tiny and changed sign between v1's split and cross-fitting.

Why not regression adjustment for the evaluation?

Arbour et al. (2026) show it reduces variance when features predict the outcome. Here they explain about 2.7% of visit variance, so the gain would be negligible. We note it and did not implement it.

Would this work for a catalog or a voucher?

Unknown. The tested intervention is an email. A costlier channel needs its own randomised pilot.

What would you recommend the retailer do?

For visits, send to past women's buyers ranked by history, because it matches the models and is transparent. Keep a random holdout so the next campaign can test it again.

Which email should be sent if both are available?

In our IPW extension the targeted men's-email list gave +9.3 pp [7.4, 11.3] and the targeted women's-email list +7.9 pp [6.3, 9.6]. Even the men's email sent at random gave +8.3 pp. The gaps among these policies are not established. One fold seed only.

How does IPW work here?

Arms were assigned with known shares (about 33% each). A policy's value is the weighted average outcome of customers whose actual arm matches what the policy would send them, weighted by one over the arm share. Self-normalised. We subtract the no-email value and divide by the share contacted.

17. How to run and reproduce NEW

You need uv, a Python project tool. It keeps everything inside the project folder in .venv. Nothing is installed globally. Install it from docs.astral.sh/uv if you do not have it.

Open a terminal in the project folder, then:

uv sync                      # once: create .venv with the locked package versions
uv run python run_all.py     # analysis, slides, notes, number check, this page (2 to 4 min)

It should end with All numbers trace to results.json and Saved .../PROJECT_GUIDE.html. Runs are seeded, so you get the same numbers every time.

Rebuild slides and notes onlyuv run python slides/build_slides_v2.py
Rebuild this page onlyuv run python make_guide.py
Check every slide numberuv run python verify_numbers.py
See all optionsuv run python prospect_selection_v2.py --help

20. Glossary

RCT (randomised controlled trial)
People are assigned to groups at random. Groups differ only by chance and by the treatment, so outcome gaps are caused by the treatment.
Arm
One random group: no email, men's email, women's email.
Treated / emailed
Got the women's email.
Control / not emailed
Got no email.
Visit
Customer visited the website within two weeks. Primary outcome.
Conversion
Customer bought within two weeks.
Spend
Dollars spent in two weeks. Gross revenue, not profit.
Cap q
Maximum share of customers the retailer may email. Default 15.6%.
K
The brief's name for the limit. Here K = q x number of customers.
Policy
A rule or model that ranks customers. The top q get the email.
Shortlist / list
The customers a policy picks.
Lift
Inside a list: mean outcome of emailed minus mean outcome of not emailed. The email's effect on that list.
pp (percentage points)
Difference between two percentages. 15% minus 10% = 5 pp.
Response model
Predicts the chance of visiting if emailed. Favours people who would visit anyway.
Uplift model
Predicts the change in visit chance caused by the email.
CATE
Conditional average treatment effect. The uplift for customers with given features.
T-learner
Uplift model using two models, one per arm. Score = difference.
X-learner
Uplift model that imputes each customer's missing outcome, then models the difference. The v1 model.
RFM
Recency, frequency, monetary. Classic marketing ranking. Here: past 12-month spend.
HGB
HistGradientBoosting. A tree-boosting model from scikit-learn.
Isotonic calibration
A monotone adjustment of predicted probabilities so they match observed rates.
Brier score
Mean squared error of predicted probabilities. Lower is better.
Cross-fitting
Score each fold with models trained on the other folds. No customer is scored by a model that saw them.
Fold
One of the equal parts the data is split into.
Stratified split
A split that keeps the mix of key groups the same in every part.
Fold seed / repeat
The random number that decides the fold split. Different seeds give different splits.
Canonical repeat
The one fold seed used for intervals and figures (seed 0).
Bootstrap
Resample the data with replacement many times and recompute. The spread shows uncertainty.
95% CI (confidence interval)
A range of plausible values. If it includes 0, we cannot say the effect or difference is real.
Paired difference
Two policies compared on the same bootstrap samples. Sharper than comparing separate intervals.
SD (standard deviation)
How spread out values are. Here: how much a result moves across fold seeds.
SE (standard error)
SD of an estimate across bootstrap samples. Its uncertainty.
z
Difference divided by its SE. Around 2 or more usually counts as clear.
Jaccard overlap
Customers in both lists divided by customers in either. 1 = identical, 0 = no overlap.
Profile
Average features of the customers on a list.
Qini curve
Cumulative extra visits as you email more customers in ranked order.
SMD
Standardised mean difference between arms. Below 0.10 means they look alike.
Margin
Share of revenue left after product cost. Not in the data. Assumed 50%.
Break-even cost
Margin x spend lift. The most one email can cost without losing money.
IPW (inverse-probability weighting)
Scores a policy using customers whose random arm matched the policy's choice, weighted by 1 / arm share.
Hajek estimator
IPW where weights are normalised to sum to one. More stable.
R squared
Share of outcome variation the features explain. Here very small.
Regression adjustment
Using features to reduce noise when comparing groups. Helps only if features predict the outcome well.
Out of fold
Predictions made by models that did not train on that row.
Legacy mode
v2 running the v1 protocol (one split, seed 42, top 1,500) to reproduce v1 exactly.
uv
A Python tool that creates a project-local environment from a lock file.
Seed
A fixed starting number for randomness. Same seed, same result.
